01.note: Rabbi Eliezer went to visit his disciple Rabbi Yosei ben Perida in the town of Ovelin and found him living in an alleyway that had only one side post. He told him: My son, set up another side post. The disciple answered: Am I required to close it up? Rabbi Eliezer replied: Let it be closed up; what does it matter?
01.why: The Gemara asks whether Rabbi Eliezer wants two side posts plus a cross beam, or two side posts alone. It reads the disciple's 'close it up' as showing a cross beam was also required, then rejects the proof: he may have meant closing it with side posts.

people.name: Rabbi Eliezer
people.about: A teacher who visits his disciple and tells him to add a second side post to his alleyway.

people.name: Rabbi Yosei ben Perida
people.about: Rabbi Eliezer's disciple, living in Ovelin in an alleyway with only one side post.

terms.meaning: An upright post at the entrance of an alleyway. It marks the alley off from the public street so that people may carry objects within it on Shabbat.
A collection of early rabbinic teachings from the same period as the Mishna, often adding cases and details the Mishna leaves out.

02.note: Rabbi Meir, a scribe who wrote Torah scrolls, studied with two great teachers, Rabbi Yishmael and Rabbi Akiva. In one account he put iron sulfate in his ink, and Rabbi Yishmael said nothing while Rabbi Akiva forbade it. In a second account it is the reverse: Rabbi Yishmael asked his trade, warned him that adding or leaving out one letter could destroy the whole world, and when Meir said he used iron sulfate so his ink would not be erased, Yishmael objected that the Torah requires writing that can be blotted out.
02.why: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi has just said that the unnamed disciple who studied under both Rabbi Yishmael and Rabbi Akiva is Rabbi Meir; this teaching is brought to show he served both. The Gemara then notes the two accounts disagree on which teacher came first and which one forbade the ink.

people.name: Rabbi Meir
people.about: A scribe of Torah scrolls who studied under both Rabbi Yishmael and Rabbi Akiva.

people.name: Rabbi Yishmael
people.about: One of Rabbi Meir's teachers; in one account he warns him to take great care as a scribe.

people.name: Rabbi Akiva
people.about: Rabbi Meir's other teacher; the two accounts disagree on whether he forbade the iron sulfate.

terms.meaning: A chemical added to ink that makes it permanent and hard to erase.
A teaching from the early rabbinic period that was not included in the Mishna, the core law code the Talmud discusses.
A wife suspected by her husband of adultery. In the Torah's ritual, a priest writes curses on a scroll and dissolves the writing into water she drinks, which is why that ink must be erasable.

03.note: For three years the two great schools, Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel, disagreed, each saying the law followed its own view. Then a Divine Voice came out and declared that both are the words of the living God, but the law follows Beit Hillel. The Gemara asks why Beit Hillel won, and answers that they were agreeable and forbearing, taught their opponents' views alongside their own, and even mentioned Beit Shammai's opinion first.
03.why: The discussion has just praised a student so clever he could argue a creeping animal pure. This story says Beit Hillel won the law through humility, not sharpness, and the Gemara goes on to show them naming Beit Shammai's elders first in a mishna.

people.name: Rabbi Abba
people.about: Reports this account in the name of Shmuel.

people.name: Shmuel
people.about: The Sage in whose name the account is told.

terms.meaning: The two leading schools of early rabbinic law, named for their founders Shammai and Hillel, who disagreed on hundreds of questions.
A voice from heaven that, in rabbinic stories, announces God's will or settles a matter.
Jewish law; the ruling people actually follow in practice.

04.note: Rav was sitting in an alleyway with his student Rav Huna, and sent his attendant to bring a pitcher of water. While the attendant was gone, the side post at the alley's entrance fell down. Rav signaled with his hand, and the attendant stopped where he stood. Rav Huna asked why they could not rely on the palm tree at the entrance as a side post. Rav said Rav Huna was like someone who does not know the Sages' teachings: they had not relied on the palm tree since yesterday.
04.why: The Gemara is debating whether something not put up to be a side post can count as one. It infers from Rav's answer that had they relied on the palm tree before Shabbat, it would have been valid.

people.name: Rav
people.about: A Sage sitting in the alleyway who stops his attendant once the side post falls.

people.name: Rav Huna
people.about: Sits before Rav and asks why the palm tree cannot serve as the side post.

terms.meaning: An upright post at the entrance of an alleyway. It marks the alley off from the public street so that people may carry objects within it on Shabbat; without it, carrying there is forbidden.
A narrow lane shared by several houses that opens onto a public street. Special rules decide when carrying is allowed in it on Shabbat.

05.note: Rav Nahman taught in public, in Shmuel's name, that one traveler or two may enclose two beit se'a with ropes, and three, who count as a caravan, may enclose six. He was asked whether he had abandoned the majority of the Rabbis to follow the lone view of Rabbi Yosei, son of Rabbi Yehuda. Rav Nahman then set up a speaker beside him and announced: What I told you was my error. Three people get as much space as they need. The Gemara then explains that the first half still follows Rabbi Yosei because his father, Rabbi Yehuda, held the same view.
05.why: The Gemara has been comparing Rabbi Yosei, son of Rabbi Yehuda, with the Rabbis on how much space ropes may enclose for travelers. Rav Nahman's public correction shows which view the law follows for a caravan.

people.name: Rav Nahman
people.about: Teaches a ruling in Shmuel's name, then publicly retracts part of it as his own error.

people.name: Shmuel
people.about: The Sage in whose name Rav Nahman first taught, called here 'Rabbeinu', our teacher.

people.name: Rabbi Yosei, son of Rabbi Yehuda
people.about: An early Sage whose minority view Rav Nahman was accused of following.

people.name: Rabbi Yehuda
people.about: Father of Rabbi Yosei; the Gemara says he held the same view as his son.

terms.meaning: An area of land, the space in which a se'a of seed is sown; roughly 50 by 50 cubits. Two beit se'a is the standard size of an enclosure one may carry in on Shabbat.
A group of three or more travelers, who are given more space to enclose for carrying on Shabbat than one or two people.
A man who stood by a teacher and repeated his words aloud to the audience. Setting one up made Rav Nahman's correction an official public lecture.

06.note: Rav Hisda said to Marei, son of Rav Huna and grandson of Rav Yirmeya bar Abba: People say you walk on Shabbat from Barnish to Daniel's synagogue, three parasangs away. What do you rely on, the huts at the edge of town? Your own grandfather said in Rav's name that the law of huts does not apply in Babylonia. Marei went out and showed him a line of ruined towns, each within seventy cubits and a bit of the next, which he relied on instead.
06.why: The Gemara has just cited Rav, through Rav Yirmeya bar Abba, that huts do not extend the Shabbat boundary in Babylonia. Rav Hisda tests the grandson against his grandfather's ruling, and Marei shows he relied on something else.

people.name: Rav Hisda
people.about: Questions Marei about his long Shabbat walk.

people.name: Marei
people.about: Son of Rav Huna and grandson of Rav Yirmeya bar Abba; walks from Barnish to Daniel's synagogue on Shabbat.

people.name: Rav Yirmeya bar Abba
people.about: Marei's grandfather, who reported in Rav's name that the law of huts does not apply in Babylonia.

terms.meaning: A Persian unit of distance, about four miles. Three parasangs is far beyond the normal 2,000-cubit walking limit on Shabbat.
Simple dwellings outside a town. Where they count as homes, the town's Shabbat boundary is measured from them, letting people walk farther.
The distance, about seventy and two-thirds cubits, within which separate settlements are treated as one town when measuring the Shabbat walking limit.

07.note: Rabbi Akiva was held in prison, and Rabbi Yehoshua HaGarsi looked after him, bringing a measured amount of water each day. One day the guard said the water was too much, perhaps to dig through the prison wall, and poured out half. When Rabbi Akiva saw how little there was, he said: Do you not know I am old and my life depends on yours? Hearing what happened, he still asked for water to wash his hands. Rabbi Yehoshua protested that there was not enough even to drink. Rabbi Akiva said it was better to die his own death than go against his colleagues' ruling, and he tasted nothing until he had washed. The Sages said: if he is so careful in old age and in prison, how much more so in youth and in freedom.
07.why: The Gemara has been stressing how weighty the words of the Sages are, saying that whoever mocks them is punished. Handwashing before eating is one of their rules, and right after the story the Gemara credits King Solomon with instituting it.

people.name: Rabbi Akiva
people.about: Imprisoned and old; insists on washing his hands before eating even when water is scarce.

people.name: Rabbi Yehoshua HaGarsi
people.about: Attends to Rabbi Akiva in prison and brings him his daily water.

terms.meaning: A ritual rinsing of the hands before eating bread, enacted by the Sages. Rabbi Akiva here treats breaking it as deserving death.
A teaching from the early rabbinic period that was not included in the Mishna, the core law code the Talmud discusses.

08.note: Rav Adda bar Mattana was about to leave for the study hall when his wife asked him: What shall I do for your children? He answered: Are all the rushes in the marsh already gone? Let them eat those.
08.why: The Gemara is reading 'black as a raven' in the Song of Songs as describing who keeps the Torah. Rava says it is one who is cruel to his family like a raven for the Torah's sake, and this exchange is his example.

people.name: Rav Adda bar Mattana
people.about: A scholar who leaves for the study hall and tells his wife to feed the children rushes.

people.name: Rava
people.about: The Sage who gives this as an example of making oneself cruel to one's household for Torah.

terms.meaning: Marsh plants, a poor famine food. Rav Adda is saying the children can eat those if there is nothing else.

09.note: A woman built a partition on top of an existing partition on land that had belonged to a convert who died. Then a man came and plowed the ground a little. He brought the matter to Rav Nahman, who ruled the land belonged to him. The woman came and cried out before Rav Nahman, and he told her: What can I do for you? You did not take possession the way people take possession.
09.why: The Gemara has been discussing partitions added on top of existing ones, and whether they count. This case from property law shows Rav Nahman did not count such added building as a real act of taking ownership.

people.name: Rav Nahman
people.about: The judge who awards the land to the man who plowed it.

terms.meaning: A convert who died with no Jewish heirs left property that belonged to no one, so the first person to take possession of it could acquire it.
Doing something to ownerless land, such as working it, that legally makes it yours.

10.note: An orchard bordered on the wall of a mansion, and that wall also served as one of the orchard's walls. The mansion's outer wall collapsed. Rav Beivai thought the mansion's inner walls could be used as the orchard's wall instead. Rav Pappi mocked him: Because you come from truncated people, you say truncated things. Those walls were built for the inside of the mansion, not for the outside.
10.why: The Gemara has been asking whether a fallen wall leaves an enclosure in which carrying is still allowed. This case asks whether walls built for another purpose, the mansion's interior, can close the gap; Rav Pappi says they cannot.

people.name: Rav Beivai
people.about: Proposes using the mansion's inner walls to enclose the orchard.

people.name: Rav Pappi
people.about: Rejects Rav Beivai's idea with a cutting pun about his family.

terms.meaning: A pun. The translation explains that Rav Beivai's family descended from the priest Eli, whose descendants were said to die young, so Rav Pappi calls his idea 'cut short' too.

11.note: The Exilarch had a banqueting pavilion in his orchard and asked Rav Huna bar Hinnana to arrange for them to eat there the next day, Shabbat. Rav Huna bar Hinnana put up fences of reeds set less than three handbreadths apart. Rava went and pulled them out, and his students Rav Pappa and Rav Huna, son of Rav Yehoshua, gathered up the reeds after him. The next day Ravina, then Rav Pappa and Rav Huna, son of Rav Yehoshua, each raised objections to Rava, showing the fences had been needed. The Exilarch applied a verse to them: They are wise to do evil, but to do good they have no knowledge.
11.why: The Gemara has been asking when a large enclosure counts as enclosed for living, which permits carrying. Rava treated the orchard as residential because of the pavilion; the objections from new and old towns and from privacy screens argue it was not.

people.name: Exilarch
people.about: Owner of the orchard and pavilion, who wanted to eat there on Shabbat.

people.name: Rav Huna bar Hinnana
people.about: Builds the reed fences at the Exilarch's request.

people.name: Rava
people.about: Removes the reed fences, judging them unnecessary.

people.name: Rav Pappa
people.about: Rava's student; collects the reeds, then the next day raises an objection to Rava.

people.name: Ravina
people.about: Objects to Rava the next day from the rule about new and old towns.

terms.meaning: The head of the Jewish community in Babylonia, a powerful leader with his own court.
A measure of about the width of a palm. Reeds set less than three handbreadths apart count in Jewish law as a solid wall.
A legal arrangement that joins several homes or courtyards into one shared space, so that people may carry between them on Shabbat.
The distance one may walk outside a town on Shabbat, measured from its edge; the new-town and old-town rule decides where that edge is.

12.note: When Rabbi Zeira was too tired to study, he would sit at the entrance of Rav Yehuda bar Ami's academy, so he could stand up for the Sages as they came and went and earn reward for honoring them. Once a schoolchild came out, and Rabbi Zeira asked what his teacher had taught him. The child said the blessing over dodder is 'Who creates the fruit of the ground', and over green grain 'By Whose word all things came to be'. Rabbi Zeira said the opposite made more sense, since green grain draws its food from the ground and dodder from the air.
12.why: The Gemara has just discussed green grain as food for an eiruv. After the story it rules that the law follows the child: dodder is fully ripened produce and green grain is not, and dodder does draw from the ground, since it dies when its host shrub is cut.

people.name: Rabbi Zeira
people.about: A Sage who rests at an academy door to honor scholars and questions a schoolchild.

people.name: Rav Yehuda bar Ami
people.about: Head of the academy at whose entrance Rabbi Zeira sits.

terms.meaning: A climbing plant that wraps around a shrub and lives off it.
A short praise of God said before eating. The wording depends on the food: produce of the ground gets one blessing, other foods a general one.

13.note: Rabbi Hanina once ate half an onion along with half of its toxins. He fell deathly ill. His colleagues prayed for mercy for him, and he lived, because the times needed him.
13.why: The Gemara is asking whether onions can be used for an eiruv, and has explained that onion leaves can be deadly. This teaching, warning against eating onion, adds a case of a Sage nearly killed by one.

people.name: Rabbi Hanina
people.about: A Sage who nearly died after eating an onion and recovered after his colleagues prayed for him.

terms.meaning: A teaching from the early rabbinic period that was not included in the Mishna, the core law code the Talmud discusses.
His generation needed his teaching, so he was spared; otherwise, the text implies, he would not have recovered.

14.note: An army came to Neharde'a and took over the study hall, leaving the students no room. Rav Nahman told them: Go out to the marshes and make seats by pressing down reeds, and tomorrow, on Shabbat, we will go and sit on them.
14.why: The mishna says an eiruv placed on a reed counts only if the reed was cut and stuck back in the ground. Rav Nahman's instruction is challenged from that mishna, and he answers that the mishna is about hard reeds, while soft ones may be bent and used.

people.name: Rav Nahman
people.about: A Sage in Neharde'a who tells his students to make reed seats in the marsh for Shabbat study.

terms.meaning: Bending growing reeds down and binding them into seats before Shabbat, since using growing plants on Shabbat itself is restricted.

15.note: A deer was brought to the Exilarch's house, caught on the first day of a Diaspora Festival and slaughtered on the second. Rav Nahman and Rav Hisda ate it; Rav Sheshet refused. Rav Nahman joked: What can I do for Rav Sheshet, who will not eat deer? Rav Sheshet cited Isi's teaching that Rabbi Yosei forbids this on the two Diaspora Festival days. Later Rabba bar Shmuel told Rav Sheshet he had learned that Rabbi Yosei agrees about those two days, and Rav Sheshet said: If you meet them, tell them nothing. Rav Ashi reported, in Ameimar's name, that the deer was not caught on the Festival but brought from outside the Shabbat limit; in that version, the Gemara says, the meeting never happened.
15.why: A teaching just cited has Rabbi Yosei forbid treating the two Diaspora Festival days as separate, even with a condition. The deer case tests whether a Sage may rely on one of those days being an ordinary weekday.

people.name: Rav Nahman
people.about: Eats the deer and teases Rav Sheshet for refusing.

people.name: Rav Hisda
people.about: Eats the deer together with Rav Nahman.

people.name: Rav Sheshet
people.about: Refuses to eat the deer, citing a teaching attributed to Rabbi Yosei.

people.name: Rabba bar Shmuel
people.about: Tells Rav Sheshet a teaching that would undercut his refusal.

people.name: Ameimar
people.about: Tells Rav Ashi a different version: the deer was brought from outside the Shabbat limit.

terms.meaning: The head of the Jewish community in Babylonia, who often hosted the Sages at his table.

terms.term: two Festival days of the Diaspora
terms.meaning: Outside the Land of Israel, each Festival was kept for two days because of doubt about the calendar, so one of the two was really an ordinary day.
The distance, 2,000 cubits beyond a town, that one may walk or carry things on Shabbat or a Festival. Food brought from beyond it on the holy day may be forbidden.

16.note: On a Festival, a delivery of turnips arrived in the town of Mehoza. Rava went out, saw that they were withered, and allowed people to buy them, saying they must have been pulled up the day before. Even if they came from outside the Shabbat limit, what is brought for one Jew is permitted to another, and these were brought for gentiles. But once Rava saw the merchants bringing more and more turnips, he forbade them.
16.why: The Gemara has just explained that the Sages disagreed over the deer at the Exilarch's house about whether food brought from outside the limit for one person is allowed to others. Rava's ruling applies that principle, and shows its limit once goods are brought for Jews.

people.name: Rava
people.about: A Sage in Mehoza who first permits buying the turnips and later forbids it.

terms.meaning: The distance, 2,000 cubits beyond a town, that one may walk or carry things on Shabbat or a Festival. Goods brought from beyond it for a Jew on the holy day are forbidden to him.
A biblical holy day, such as Passover or Sukkot, on which most work is forbidden as on Shabbat.

17.note: Some canopy makers cut myrtle branches on the second day of a Festival, and that evening Ravina allowed people to smell them right away. Rava bar Tahalifa told Ravina to forbid it, since these men were not learned in Torah. Rav Shemaya objected: even for the learned, don't we require waiting as long as it would take to cut them? They went and asked Rava, who said: We require that wait.
17.why: The Gemara is collecting cases of goods prepared or brought on a Festival and when they may be used. This one asks whether people must wait after the Festival for the time it took to do the forbidden work.

people.name: Ravina
people.about: Permits smelling the myrtles immediately after the Festival.

people.name: Rava bar Tahalifa
people.about: Urges Ravina to forbid it because the canopy makers are not learned.

people.name: Rav Shemaya
people.about: Argues that a waiting period applies to everyone.

people.name: Rava
people.about: Rules that one must wait as long as it took to cut the myrtles.

terms.meaning: Outside the Land of Israel, each Festival was kept for two days because of doubt about the calendar.
After a holy day ends, something made forbiddenly on it may be used only after waiting as long as it would take to do that work.

18.note: The Sages sent Rav Yeimar the Elder to Rav Hisda on the eve of Rosh HaShana, telling him to watch what he did and report back. When Rav Hisda saw him, he quoted a folk saying: One who picks up a damp log wants to do something on the spot, meaning: you have come for a reason. They brought him a cup of wine, and he recited kiddush and the blessing for time.
18.why: The Gemara has been asking whether the blessing for time is said on Rosh HaShana and Yom Kippur, and how, since one cannot drink wine on Yom Kippur. Rav Hisda's practice settles it: the blessing is said on both days, even without wine.

people.name: Rav Yeimar the Elder
people.about: Sent by the Sages to see how Rav Hisda conducts himself on the eve of Rosh HaShana.

people.name: Rav Hisda
people.about: Recites kiddush and the blessing for time over wine as Rav Yeimar watches.

terms.meaning: A blessing said over a cup of wine at the start of Shabbat or a Festival, declaring the day holy.
The blessing thanking God 'Who has given us life' and brought us to this season, said at the start of a Festival.
The Jewish New Year, a two-day holy day in the autumn.

19.note: After Rabban Gamliel died, Rabbi Yehoshua came into the study hall to overturn his ruling on fasts. Rabbi Yohanan ben Nuri stood up and said: The body follows the head. All of Rabban Gamliel's life we fixed the law according to him, and now you want to cancel his words? Yehoshua, we will not listen to you; the law has been fixed according to Rabban Gamliel. And no one disputed this at all.
19.why: Ulla rules with Rabbi Yosei that a Ninth of Av fast falling on Friday is completed; Rabban Gamliel's view, as Rabbi Meir reports it, is that it is not. The Gemara cites this to show Rabban Gamliel's ruling became law, then answers that in Rabbi Yosei's time people followed Rabbi Yosei.

people.name: Rabban Gamliel
people.about: Leader of the Sages, whose rulings were followed throughout his life; the story begins after his death.

people.name: Rabbi Yehoshua
people.about: Tries to overturn Rabban Gamliel's ruling after his death.

people.name: Rabbi Yohanan ben Nuri
people.about: Stands up to defend Rabban Gamliel's ruling against Rabbi Yehoshua.

terms.meaning: A teaching from the early rabbinic period that was not included in the Mishna, the core law code the Talmud discusses.
A saying meaning the community should follow its established leaders and the rulings already fixed by them.

20.note: Rabban Gamliel and others were traveling by boat, and it did not reach port until after nightfall on Friday, when Shabbat had begun. They asked Rabban Gamliel whether they could get off. He said they could, because he had been watching and knew they had come within the city's limit before nightfall, so they could walk anywhere in the city.
20.why: Right afterward the Gemara explains how Rabban Gamliel could tell: he had a tube he looked through to judge 2,000 cubits on land and the same distance at sea.

people.name: Rabban Gamliel
people.about: Rules that the passengers may leave the boat, having watched when it came within the city's limit.

terms.meaning: On Shabbat one may walk 2,000 cubits beyond the place where one was when Shabbat began. Arriving inside that range before nightfall let the passengers go through the whole city.

20.flag: The STORY segment is only the Gemara quoting the opening words of a mishna ('On one occasion they did not enter the port, etc.'); the events come from the translator's expansion, not from the segment's own text.
